docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm Harsh Kanth. For more than ten years, I've helped companies explain their products clearly, from SAP enterprise software to Microsoft's developer platform to startups writing their first help center.

Today I work as an SAP consultant and technical writer, consult on documentation for identity and enterprise software teams, and train and evaluate AI models on technical writing. I use AI tools like Claude and SAP Joule every day: to review my work and, from time to time, to explore ideas or rough out a first draft that I then refine, along with AI-assisted checks in VS Code and GitHub.

My work covers the whole documentation lifecycle: planning the information architecture, writing and testing the content, setting the style, building the publishing pipeline, and keeping it all current release after release.

docs.title: What I believe about documentation
docs.text:
Documentation is part of the product. Users meet it at the moments that decide whether they succeed: installing, configuring, recovering from an error. It deserves the same care as the interface.

Terminology is a design decision. Most confusing documentation isn't badly written; it uses three words for one thing. Agreeing on terms early saves every reader time later.

Structure beats volume. A smaller set of well-organized, task-focused topics helps more than a large set of pages nobody can navigate.

Docs should be easy to maintain. Version control, templates, and content reuse keep documentation accurate long after the first release.

docs.title: Why docs as code
docs.text:
Documentation that lives in the same tools as the product keeps up with the product. Writing in Markdown and managing it in Git gives documentation the same advantages code has:

  • Every change is tracked. Git history shows what changed, when, and why.
  • Review happens in pull requests. Engineers and product owners can comment on the exact line, or suggest a fix themselves.
  • The build checks the work. A strict build fails on broken links, missing pages, and invalid configuration before anything is published.
  • Publishing is automatic. Merging to the main branch is the release. Nobody uploads files by hand.

docs.title: The publishing pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[I write in Markdown<br/>VS Code] --> B[AI review: structure,<br/>style, formatting]
  B --> C[Commit and open<br/>a pull request]
  C --> D[Human review<br/>and merge]
  D --> E[GitHub Actions<br/>mkdocs build --strict]
  E --> F[GitHub Pages<br/>harshkanth.com]

The deploy workflow is short enough to read in full:

.github/workflows/deploy.yml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
      - run: mkdocs gh-deploy --force

docs.title: How the repository is organized
docs.text:
harsh-kanth/
├── mkdocs.yml              # site settings, navigation, theme
├── requirements.txt        # pinned MkDocs and Material versions
├── overrides/              # small template changes (sharing metadata)
├── .github/workflows/      # build and deploy on every merge
└── docs/
    ├── index.md            # home page
    ├── work/               # one Markdown file per case study
    ├── samples/            # complete writing samples
    ├── experience.md
    ├── services.md
    ├── docs-as-code.md     # this page
    └── assets/             # stylesheet, images, résumé

Adding a case study means adding one Markdown file and one line to mkdocs.yml. The structure is documented in the repository's README, so the site is as maintainable as the documentation I hand over to clients.

docs.title: How I use AI
docs.text:
AI is part of how I work, used where it helps. Most of the time it reviews what I've written. Sometimes I bring it in earlier, to explore ideas or get a rough first draft, which I then rework and refine in my own words. Either way, I decide what stays.

  • review

    Review and consistency

    Checking pages for clarity, consistency, and terminology, and catching what's easy to miss on my own read.

  • ideas and drafts

    Ideas and first drafts

    Brainstorming angles and outlines, or getting a rough first draft to react to, then rewriting and refining it myself.

  • structure and style

    Structure, style, and formatting

    Suggestions on section order and headings, checks against style rules, and clean Markdown, tables, and code blocks.

  • tools

    What I use

    AI assistants for drafting help and review, plus AI-assisted checks in VS Code and on GitHub pull requests.

docs.title: My rules for AI
docs.text:
• I own the content. Whether AI suggested an idea, drafted a section, or reviewed a page, the final wording and the decisions are mine.
  • Drafts are a starting point. Anything AI drafts gets reworked and refined before it goes anywhere.
  • Facts come from the source. Steps, values, and claims are checked against the product or the subject matter expert, never taken from a model.
  • Confidential stays confidential. Client material goes only into tools the client has approved.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
I help software teams ship documentation that's accurate, consistent, and easy to maintain, and write content that explains their products to everyone else. I work as an embedded writer, a consultant on a defined project, or a long-term documentation owner.

  • Product documentation

    Installation, admin, and user guides, product assistance, and release notes for SaaS and enterprise products.

  • API and developer documentation

    REST and GraphQL references, SDK and integration guides, authentication flows, and Swagger/OpenAPI content.

  • Documentation architecture

    Portal structure and taxonomy, templates, content reuse, and migration to docs as code with AI-assisted review.

  • Style guides, governance, and audits

    House style guides, terminology management, and review workflows, plus audits of existing docs with a prioritized plan.

  • Content writing

    Articles, whitepapers, case studies, web copy, and ghostwritten content that explains technical ideas to a wider audience.

  • Training and enablement

    Video training, onboarding content, SOPs, and knowledge transfer so your team can maintain the docs.

docs.title: Ways to work together
docs.text: Engagement Best for Project A defined deliverable, such as a product launch doc set, an API reference, or a portal migration Retainer Ongoing documentation ownership alongside your release cycle Audit A clear picture of what's working, what isn't, and what to fix first

docs.title: How a project runs
docs.text:
1. Discovery. I learn the product, the readers, and the release plan, and review any existing docs.
  2. Plan. You get an outline, a terminology list, and a schedule before writing starts.
  3. Write and test. I write against the real product and test every procedure.
  4. Review. Your SMEs and product owners review in a lightweight loop, in Git, Confluence, or Word.
  5. Publish and hand over. The docs go live on your platform, with templates and guidance so they stay current.

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
When you read these samples, notice the patterns I apply across all my documentation:

  • One task per page. Each guide has a single goal stated in its first sentence.
  • Prerequisites up front. Readers know what they need before they start, not halfway through.
  • Numbered steps with one action each. UI labels are in bold and match the product exactly.
  • A result after each procedure. Readers can confirm that the task worked.
  • Troubleshooting close to the task. The most common failures are covered on the same page.

For larger, real-world projects, see Work.

docs.title: Install Microsoft Teams
docs.text:
Install Microsoft Teams on your computer or phone and sign in, so you can chat, meet, and share files with your team.

Writing sample

This guide was written as a portfolio sample and is not official Microsoft documentation. Product screens and options can change; for the latest details, see Microsoft Support.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Make sure you have the following:

  • A device running a supported operating system: Windows 10 or 11, macOS, Android, or iOS
  • A stable internet connection
  • A Microsoft account, or a work or school account provided by your organization
  • Permission to install apps on the device. On a work computer, your IT team may need to install Teams for you.

docs.title: Step 1: Download Teams
docs.text:
1. Go to the Microsoft Teams download page.

  2. Select the download for your device.

    WindowsmacOSAndroid and iOS

    Select Download for desktop, and then select the Windows download.

    Select Download for desktop, and then select the macOS download.

    Install Microsoft Teams from Google Play or the App Store, and then go to Step 3.

docs.title: Step 2: Install Teams
docs.text:
WindowsmacOS
  1. Open your Downloads folder and double-click the Teams installer.
  2. If Windows asks whether to allow the app to make changes, select Yes.
  3. Follow the on-screen instructions.

When installation finishes, Teams opens automatically.

  1. Open your Downloads folder and double-click the Teams .pkg file.
  2. Follow the steps in the installer, and enter your Mac password if prompted.

When installation finishes, Teams appears in your Applications folder.

docs.title: Step 3: Sign in
docs.text:
1. Open Teams.
  2. Enter the email address for your Microsoft account or your work or school account, and then select Next.
  3. Enter your password, and complete any additional verification your organization requires.

  4. On the welcome screen, confirm your name and select Continue.

    Confirm your account and select Continue.

Result: Teams opens to the Chat tab, and you're ready to start working.

docs.title: Step 4: Check your audio and notifications (recommended)
docs.text:
Take a minute to set up the basics before your first call.

  1. Select Settings and more (...) next to your profile picture, and then select Settings.
  2. Select Devices, choose your speaker, microphone, and camera, and then select Make a test call.
  3. Select Notifications and activity, and choose how you want to be notified about chats, mentions, and meetings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Teams doesn't open after installation

Restart your device and open Teams again. On Windows, check that Teams isn't already running in the system tray, near the clock.

The installer won't run on my work computer

Your organization might restrict app installations. Contact your IT team, or use Teams in a browser at teams.microsoft.com in the meantime.

I can't sign in with my work account

Confirm that you're using the email address your organization gave you, and that your organization has Teams enabled. If you still can't sign in, contact your IT team.

docs.title: Schedule a meeting in Microsoft Teams
docs.text:
Schedule a Teams meeting from your calendar, invite people inside or outside your organization, and control who can present and who waits in the lobby.

Writing sample

This guide was written as a portfolio sample and is not official Microsoft documentation. Product screens and options can change; for the latest details, see Microsoft Support.

Who this is for: anyone who needs to set up one-on-one meetings, team meetings, or meetings with external guests.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Install Teams, or open it in a browser at teams.microsoft.com. For setup steps, see Install Microsoft Teams.
  • Use a work or school account. Your organization's settings control whether you can schedule meetings and invite external guests.

docs.title: Open Teams and sign in
docs.text:
1. Open the Teams app, or go to teams.microsoft.com in your browser.

  2. Sign in with your work or school account.

  3. On the welcome screen, select Continue.

Result: Teams opens to the Chat tab.

docs.title: Create the meeting
docs.text:
1. In the left navigation, select Calendar.
  2. In the top-right corner of the calendar, select New meeting.

  3. Enter the meeting details:

    Field What to enter Title A short, specific name, for example "Q3 roadmap review" Required attendees Names or email addresses. Teams suggests people from your organization as you type. To invite someone outside your organization, enter their full email address. Date and time The start and end times. Select Scheduling Assistant to see when attendees are free. Location Leave blank for an online-only meeting, or add a room for a hybrid meeting. Details The agenda, plus any documents or links people should review beforehand.

  4. Optional: to repeat the meeting, select Does not repeat and choose how often it should recur.

docs.title: Set meeting options (optional)
docs.text:
Meeting options control what happens when people join. You can set them now or any time before the meeting.

  1. Save the meeting first, then open it from your calendar.
  2. Select Meeting options.
  3. Choose your settings, for example:
    • Who can bypass the lobby: decide who joins directly and who waits for you to admit them.
    • Who can present: limit presenting to you or to specific people.
    • Allow mic and camera for attendees: turn off for large broadcasts.
  4. Select Save.

Tip

For meetings with external guests, have them wait in the lobby and limit who can present. You can admit people and change roles during the meeting.

docs.title: Send the invitation
docs.text:
1. Review the details.
  2. Select Send, or Save if you haven't invited anyone yet.

Result: attendees receive an invitation with the date, time, and a Join link. The meeting appears in your Teams calendar and in Outlook.

docs.title: Join or update the meeting
docs.text:
• To join, select the meeting in your calendar, and then select Join.
  • To change the meeting, open it from your calendar, make your changes, and then select Send update. Attendees receive the updated invitation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
I don't see New meeting in my calendar

Your organization might not allow you to schedule meetings. Contact your IT team.

External guests can't join

Your organization's settings might block external participants. Ask your IT team whether external access and anonymous join are allowed.

My meeting doesn't show up in Outlook

Make sure you're signed in to Teams and Outlook with the same work account, and that the Teams Meeting add-in is enabled in Outlook.

docs.title: AI training and evaluation
docs.text:
I help train AI models to write better technical content. I build pipelines, write and review outputs, evaluate them against documentation standards, and turn my findings into feedback that goes into the next round of training.

ProjectsUber, Outlier Project Aether, Mercor Project Odin RolesWriter, reviewer, evaluator FocusTechnical writing StatusOngoing

docs.title: Why a technical writer
docs.text: Models learn what good looks like from the people who judge their output. Judging technical writing well takes the same skills as writing it: knowing whether a procedure actually works, whether the structure fits the reader's task, and whether the terminology is consistent. That's ten years of documentation work applied to a new kind of reader.

  • Hands-on experience building and iterating on AI pipelines, the same skills I bring to AI-assisted documentation workflows

Confidentiality

Details of these projects are covered by confidentiality agreements, so this page describes my role rather than the work itself.

docs.title: Avancer documentation consulting
docs.text:
As documentation consultant for Avancer, an identity governance company, I own documentation across several products: a complete suite for the IGA Application Onboarding Hub, the house style guide that keeps every product consistent, and the move of the documentation from Microsoft 365 to Confluence.

ClientAvancer RoleDocumentation consultant ProductsIGA Application Onboarding Hub, Identity Bridge, NELM PlatformsMicrosoft 365 to Confluence Cloud, Word, ServiceNow Store StatusOngoing

docs.title: The challenge
docs.text: Avancer's documentation had grown product by product, with each guide developing its own habits and living in Microsoft 365. Identity governance products also have several distinct readers: IAM administrators who install and configure, application owners who respond to onboarding requests, and buyers who need to understand the value first. Every document had to describe the same products in the same words.

docs.title: A complete suite for the IGA Application Onboarding Hub
docs.text:
• Install and configure

    Installation Guide, IAM Admin Guide, and a Solution Architecture document

  • Day-to-day use

    Application Owner Guide and user guides written around the tasks each role performs

  • Connect the ecosystem

    Discovery source prerequisites for Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, and PingOne, plus AI provider setup for OpenAI, Azure, AWS, Google Vertex AI, and private LLMs

  • Explain the value

    A product brief, taken through several design iterations, and the ServiceNow Store listing copy

docs.title: Migration from Microsoft 365 to Confluence
docs.text: I moved the product documentation out of Microsoft 365 and set up the Confluence Cloud space: a clear page structure, branded PDF exports that match the Word templates, and a consistent space-wide footer. Identity Bridge documentation, including its user and connector guides, now lives and is maintained there.

docs.title: A house style guide and governance
docs.text:
• Avancer Style Guide v2.0, covering tone and voice, how to address the reader, American English, parallel construction, procedure and troubleshooting structure, and release note conventions
  • A visual identity and callout system for documents: heading hierarchy, numbered sections at every level, and consistent note, tip, and warning callouts
  • Compliance passes across release notes, user and connector guides, an Oracle to SQL Server migration guide and playbook, a TLS configuration guide, and installation, admin, and user guides
  • A seven-document set for NELM, a non-employee lifecycle management product: installation, configuration, development, and design documents, testing evidence, and a product brief

A few of the style decisions:

Topic Rule Abbreviations "for example" instead of "e.g.", "and so on" instead of "etc." Lists Oxford comma, parallel construction in every list UI actions "click" for buttons and links, "select" for options and values Inclusive terms "allowlist" and "blocklist" Release notes "Improved" instead of "Fixed", with a consistent structure per entry

docs.title: One home for the documentation
docs.text: Moving to Confluence gave the documentation a single home and page structure, which made it practical to apply the style guide and templates across the whole set instead of file by file.

docs.title: One product, several readers
docs.text: Each document in the Onboarding Hub suite maps to a single role and a single job. Admin content covers configuration, owner content covers responding to requests, and the architecture document carries the technical depth. Cross-references connect them instead of repeating content.

docs.title: Prerequisites that remove guesswork
docs.text: Integration setup is where onboarding usually stalls, so each discovery source and AI provider has its own prerequisites topic with the exact permissions, credentials, and settings to have ready before installation starts.

docs.title: A clean rename
docs.text: When the product was renamed from IARP to IGA Application Onboarding Hub, I carried the change through every document, file name, and caption in one controlled pass, so no customer-facing material used two names.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
• Owning documentation across several products, not just writing individual guides
  • Planning and running a platform migration alongside ongoing writing
  • Setting standards and making them easy for others to follow

Samples

The ServiceNow Store listing is public. Customer guides are available to Avancer customers; I can walk through redacted excerpts on request.

docs.title: Content writing and ghostwriting
docs.text:
Before and alongside documentation, I've written content that has to earn a reader's attention: articles, whitepapers, case studies, web copy, and product descriptions, often under someone else's name.

ClientsBMW USA, Amazon, Western Union, T-Mobile USA, agency clients FormatsArticles, whitepapers, case studies, web copy, product listings Years2015 – 2021 StandardChicago Manual of Style

docs.title: Why it matters for technical work
docs.text: Documentation tells a reader what to do. Content writing has to make them want to keep reading first. Writing for brands taught me to find the angle in a technical subject, to match a voice that isn't my own, and to respect a reader who can leave at any line. Those habits carry straight into product briefs, store listings, release announcements, and the introductions that decide whether anyone reads the rest of a guide.

docs.title: Selected work
docs.text:
• bmw usa / ghostwriting

    Connected vehicles and automotive innovation

    Research-driven articles, UX content, and case studies on connected vehicles and automotive technology, published under the client's name.

  • amazon / ghostwriting

    Marketplace product content

    Product descriptions and SEO copy for Amazon marketplace listings, written to sell within strict format and length rules.

  • western union / finance

    Financial services web content

    SEO-optimized web content for remittance products and digital financial services, where accuracy and plain language both matter.

  • pcc softech / telecom and education

    Web and marketing content

    Web pages, product descriptions, blogs, and whitepapers for T-Mobile USA, PCC Wireless, and education platforms, edited to the Chicago Manual of Style.

  • shoutvox / agency

    Three years of blogs, whitepapers, case studies, and manuals across finance, technology, and lifestyle, much of it ghostwritten for founders.

    Fundamentals of Technical Writing

    A complete video training module that teaches the craft to new writers, published on Coursera.

docs.title: How I approach it
docs.text:
• Find the reader's question first. A good article answers something the reader already wonders about, then earns the right to go further.
  • Learn the voice before writing. For ghostwriting, I study how the person or brand already speaks and write inside those limits.
  • Research like documentation. Claims are checked, numbers are sourced, and technical details are confirmed with subject matter experts.
  • Write for search without writing for robots. Keywords shape structure and headings; they don't replace clear sentences.

docs.title: RPA documentation, docs as code
docs.text:
EXL's iBOT robotic process automation platform had no online documentation. I proposed moving to a docs-as-code portal, then wrote the documentation from scratch and published it with Markdown, GitHub, and MkDocs.

ClientEXL Service RoleSenior technical writer (contract) Dates2025 StackMarkdown, GitHub, MkDocs, Python, VS Code

docs.title: The challenge
docs.text: An automation platform changes with every release, and documentation kept in static files falls behind quickly. Developers and QA teams needed a single place to find current workflows, integration steps, and troubleshooting, and the documentation had to be easy for engineers to review and update.

docs.title: What I delivered
docs.text:
• The proposal and the platform: an online documentation portal built on Markdown, GitHub, and MkDocs, replacing static documents
  • User manuals and troubleshooting guides for the iBOT RPA applications
  • Workflow and integration documentation for automation, orchestration, and process management, written with the RPA development team
  • Reviews and edits of content written by other team members, for quality and consistency
  • Knowledge transfer sessions on RPA concepts, documentation practice, and the new toolchain

docs.title: How I approached it
docs.text:
• Put docs where the code lives. Markdown in Git means documentation changes go through the same pull request review as code, and engineers can suggest fixes directly.
  • Write with the engineers, not after them. I worked alongside developers, QA, and project managers so procedures were confirmed against the product before publishing.
  • Leave the team self-sufficient. The KT sessions meant the portal could be maintained after my contract ended.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
• Choosing and setting up the right documentation platform, not just writing for one
  • Building a documentation set from zero under a short timeline
  • Docs-as-code fluency: Git workflows, Markdown, and static site generators. This portfolio runs on the same stack.

docs.title: Microsoft Teams developer documentation
docs.text:
Developer documentation for the Microsoft Teams platform, including the authentication section that shows developers how to add single sign-on to bots and apps. The content is public on Microsoft Learn.

ClientMicrosoft (via Ushta Te) RoleTechnical writer, tester, proofreader DatesAug 2021 – Jan 2022 AudienceApp and bot developers StandardMicrosoft Writing Style Guide

docs.title: The challenge
docs.text: Authentication is where many Teams app projects stall. Developers have to coordinate an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID (then Azure AD), the Teams app manifest, and code in their bot, and a single mismatched value breaks the flow with an unhelpful error. The documentation needed to make a multi-system setup feel linear.

docs.title: What I delivered
docs.text:
• The Add Authentication section of the Microsoft Teams developer documentation, including single sign-on for bots
  • Developer-focused topics written with engineers, product managers, and subject matter experts on the Teams platform team
  • Testing of documented procedures against the product, so every step works as written
  • Proofreading, QA, and SEO for published content, aligned with the Microsoft Writing Style Guide

docs.title: How I approached it
docs.text:
• Follow the developer's order of operations. Topics move from registering the app, to configuring the manifest, to writing code, so readers never need a value they haven't created yet.
  • Test what's written. I ran the procedures myself and wrote down the exact values and settings that worked, rather than relying on specifications.
  • Write to the house style. Microsoft's style guide favors direct, conversational instructions. Consistency with the rest of Microsoft Learn means developers trust the page immediately.

docs.title: Insurance platform documentation
docs.text:

docs.title: SAP DER MCM product assistance
docs.text:
Product assistance for Measurement Concept Management (MCM), part of SAP Distributed Energy Resources. The documentation is published on the SAP Help Portal and explains how utilities model energy communities, configure formulas, and integrate with SAP S/4HANA Utilities.

ClientSAP RoleTechnical writer, SAP consultant AudienceUtility business users, administrators, integrators Published onSAP Help Portal StatusOngoing

docs.title: The challenge
docs.text:
MCM sits at the intersection of energy regulation, metering, and billing. Readers arrive with very different mental models: a grid engineer thinks in meters and readings, a billing specialist thinks in contracts and tariffs, and an integrator thinks in APIs and processes. The product also uses precise terms that differ from the everyday language of the energy market, so loose wording leads directly to misconfiguration.

The documentation had to explain a dense domain model, stay exact about terminology, and keep up with a fast release cadence.

docs.title: What I delivered
docs.text:
• Product assistance, structured around the reader's journey: About MCM, Key Entities, Energy Communities, Configuration Types, Formulas, Managing an Energy Community, Managing Instances, Integration with SAP S/4HANA Utilities, and Authorizations
  • A new end-to-end chapter, Setting Up an Energy Community, that walks through the Tenant Electricity and Common Building Supply scenarios from first configuration to a working instance
  • App documentation for the Fiori apps used day to day, including Maintain Commercial Location Groups, Manage Commercial Models, Manage Instances, Configure Formulas, and Configure Usages
  • What's New entries and release notes for each delivery, covering features such as instance validation, pricing models and pricing agreements, actor type configuration, storage and grid actor creation, and validation events
  • API and process content, including validation event references extended from create-only to change processes, and consolidation of overlapping API content into a single guide
  • A revised business description with a concrete, scenario-based example, so evaluators can see how the product works before they configure anything

docs.title: Terminology as a product decision
docs.text: I maintain an agreed terminology set with the product owner and apply it across every topic. MCM uses commercial location rather than market location, technical location rather than metering location, technical model and commercial model rather than generic class or model names, and energy community rather than energy sharing. The difference between a tenant and a member is kept explicit everywhere it matters.

docs.title: Scenarios before reference
docs.text: Domain concepts land better when readers see them working. The energy community chapter starts from two real-world scenarios and introduces each entity only when the reader needs it, then points into the reference topics for detail.

docs.title: SAP conventions, applied consistently
docs.text: Field names, dates, and UI labels follow SAP Fiori conventions (for example, "the Valid From date"), so the documentation reads as part of the product rather than something written about it.

docs.title: Review loops with product management
docs.text: Every major topic goes through product manager review. I fold feedback in without adding speculative content, which keeps the documentation accurate to what actually ships.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
• Working fluently in a complex enterprise domain and an established corporate style
  • Owning terminology and information architecture, not just individual topics
  • Keeping release communication and core documentation in step across sprints

Samples

The published documentation is available on the SAP Help Portal. I'm happy to walk through specific topics and the structure decisions behind them.

docs.text:
Documentation explains a product; training builds the skills to use it. I create training modules and knowledge transfer sessions for writers, product users, and internal teams, often built from the same source material as the documentation.

docs.title: How I approach training
docs.text:
• Start from the task. Each module is built around something the learner needs to do, not a list of features.
  • Reuse the documentation. Training and documentation share the same terminology and source material, so they never contradict each other.
  • Show, then explain. Video walkthroughs demonstrate the task first, then cover the reasoning behind each step.
  • Leave something to come back to. Every module points to the documentation the learner will use afterwards.

docs.text:
• Turning product knowledge into structured learning, not just reference content
  • Producing video training end to end, from script to recording to LMS delivery
  • Helping teams become self-sufficient after I hand over

docs.title: Documentation overhaul across four companies
docs.text:
Vision Group runs four subsidiaries across retail technology, AI/ML, and AR/VR. As document owner reporting to the Chief Product Officer, I rebuilt how all four companies created, stored, and reused documentation.

CompanyVision Group Retail Technologies RoleLead technical writer, document owner DatesJan 2022 – Feb 2023 Reported toChief Product Officer

docs.title: The challenge
docs.text: Each subsidiary had grown its own documentation in its own place, with no shared templates or terminology. The same concepts were written several times in slightly different ways, content was hard to find, and every new document started from a blank page.

docs.title: What I delivered
docs.text:
• A documentation process with templates, styles, and a style guide used across all four subsidiaries
  • A taxonomy that organized documentation by product and audience
  • A migration of siloed content into a CMS and Git repositories
  • Content reuse so shared concepts were written once and used across products
  • New documentation for applications, servers and portals, and in-house AI software: SDK guides, API references, step-by-step feature guides, and release notes
  • Leadership of a team of technical writers and business analysts

docs.title: How I approached it
docs.text:
• Standardize first, then write. Templates and a shared style came before new content, so everything written afterwards was consistent by default.
  • Reuse instead of rewrite. Shared topics saved time and kept product descriptions aligned across the subsidiaries.
  • Make content findable. Moving documentation into a structured CMS and Git made it discoverable and easier to maintain.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
• Documentation architecture at an organizational level
  • Change management: introducing new tools and process to several teams at once
  • Owning documentation strategy with direct accountability to product leadership
